utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor versus Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I thought we had finished with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right, then. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Kuo: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness just before we broke yesterday we were discussing this piece of paper where you had written the names of people who were taken away and disappeared. The last question that was asked by the presiding judge was regarding whether this was prepared when you were being questioned by an investigator. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I prepared that list just after I got out of prison. I repeat, in order to be able to prove ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Excuse me, sir. We have a technical problem. Can you hear us now? Right. Well, you did not get any of the answer, I think, so perhaps, Ms. Kuo, you could ask the witness to repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, because of a technical problem we were not able to record your answer. Can you just repeat it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just after I was released while my memory was still fresh, in relation to the people who were taken out during the night, beaten up, and who were never returned to our rooms, I made a list of these people and I handed over that list with their names to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, we did see this typewritten list yesterday, but later in your testimony you refer to people who were taken away at the end of August, the 25th, the 27th, and then also the 30th of August. Did you prepare a separate list for that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you prepare that list? Was it also immediately after your release?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not prepare that list. I dictated that list during the investigations, to the best of my memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I'd like to have this witness shown ID 301. What is that, Witness? Is that the list that you have been referring to, that you dictated?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This list in the first part relates to people who were taken out in larger groups, about 18 or 20, in two parts. One group was taken out on the 25th of August, and the other one on the 27th of August. I cannot exactly distinguish between these people who was taken out in which group, that is, because quite a bit of time has gone by, so I can't tell now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday you gave us the names of some of those people. Does looking at this list which -- does looking at this list refresh your memory as to any other people who were taken out during that time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right now, I cannot remember any more people except for these who are mentioned here. This other part of the list relates to people who were taken out between the 30th and 31st of August because we were also taken out on the 29th and we spent the night --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, please.

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, let's just concentrate on the 25th and the 27th. My question was -- you mentioned yesterday several people taken out during that time, and you told us that you could not remember any other people unless you looked at the list. The list is before you now. Could you tell us now, in addition to the people you mentioned yesterday, were there other people that were taken out those two days, the 25th and 27th of August. Now that you've looked at the list, can you tell us from the list any other people?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember any more names except for those that I've already listed, in those two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people that you've written down on this list -- this is your handwriting, right?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many names are on the list for the 25th and 27th, written down?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 36 and 40, approximately. Not only here in terms of what I did, but those are the ones that I counted as they got out during those two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The exhibit -- I'm sorry, not the exhibit, the piece of paper before you is a little bit difficult for someone to read who can't read your handwriting. Could you just read it out to us, the names of the people from the 25th and 27th of August?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The following were taken out: Munim Kameric, Dervo Cankusic, Resko Hadzimesic, and his brother who is not entered here. Serif Hadzic, Esad Sero and two of the Nukic brothers, I don't know their names. Saban Durak, Zaim Rikalo, Hajro Sabanovic, Miralem Ramovic, Nusret Salcinovic. He was taken out exactly on the 27th, I remember that. And I remembered another one, Emsad Sabanovic. I remembered it just now because there were two Sabanovics. They were taken out on the 25th and the 27th of August, but I cannot exactly distinguish between the two groups, who was taken out on the 25th and who on the 26th, except for that one name I mentioned to you already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you also said there were 20 people taken out of the group of 55, and those 20 people were primarily younger men, and that they disappeared. Could you tell us their names now?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were in the mess hall in the restaurant where we ate, when we waited there for a long time too see what would happen to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, please just answer the question. Give us the names. We've already heard you yesterday tell us what happened. We just need the names of the 20 people.

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can mention some, but not all of them. Out of the people who were taken out with me in the direction of Niksic because I said already that we did not get any papers or anything, we didn't know where we were going to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- or what was going on. When they returned us --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, please. You have a piece of paper before you. Just tell us the names on the paper of the 20 people. I know it's not complete, but just read us the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And may I add to what counsel has said to you, sir, we really only want you to answer the questions. We have a great deal of evidence now from other sources about the matters of which you may want to speak. We only want you to answer the questions that counsel asks of you. We don't have time to hear all of this again.

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The following were taken out: Asim Mujic, Karabegovic, a taxi driver, Ismet Cemo, Ismet Pasovic, Sevko Hodzic, Emin Smajkan, Asim Nesbur and his brother, a young man nicknamed Zuga, I can't remember his real name. And then also a younger man Dudic, and a certain Mujo Rizvanovic, and Granov Murat. Those are the people who were taken out of our group in two intervals, ten by ten. All trace has been lost of them. I never received any information as to any one of these people still being alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's a second sheet to that paper and it appears there are more names. Are those more of the people taken out at that same time? Please turn the sheet over.

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These other names relate to persons who have university degrees. Mostly younger people. There are even more of them, but I just mentioned some --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, well --

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- who are missing. They also haven't been heard from since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they taken out also in that group of 20, or is that a separate group?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are separate groups. I did not mention in this group that these people were taken out. These people were taken out in separate groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people on this second sheet that you said had university degrees, when were they taken out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some were taken out during the night. Among those from the list that I read out yesterday, and others were taken out later, perhaps. I'm not sure. I cannot say exactly who was taken away when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, we're done with that piece of paper, Witness. You can put it away. Witness, you mentioned that of the people that you described as being missing, that you've never heard from them again, were you in a position such that if they were still alive, you would either -- you would know about it or have been contacted by them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were my acquaintances. They would have expressed interest in me just as I expressed interest in them. However, I haven't found out from any of their relatives or anyone that there's any hope that they had survived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you gave a statement in 1992 and to the State Commission for Gathering Facts on War Crimes, and according to that statement it says, in describing a group that was taken out on the 25th of June, 1992, that "They may have been taken to Bileca to be court martialled there but according to another version they were killed."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why -- was there ever any mention of a court martial in Bileca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Court martials were dealt with over the radio. Whether it was in Foca or Bileca I can't exactly say. To be quite frank with you, we had smuggled in a small transistor radio, and on a news programme it was said that a court martial had been established in the Crisis Staff in Foca. It was headed by Boja, a lawyer; Milic, the judge; and also Skipnja, Cedo, and Starevic. I can't remember this person's first name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And also, a Stankovic. I also don't know his first name. I didn't manage to register all of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when people were taken out and you later never heard from them, were they ever told that they were going to be court martialled in Bileca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Court martials were never referred to, only exchanges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us whether role call was taken at the detention in the evening or in the morning?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people who were taken out had their names read out from the door by a guard, and then they had to leave. Every evening in the rooms there was a role call, and the names of all of those who were present were read out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this information given to the guards at KP Dom? Were they the ones who took the role call?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The guards took the role call, and then they knew how many of us spent the night in that room. If somebody went missing during the night, the next day a new list was made out and then they would insert various things in, who you were, what you did, et cetera. So names were not repeated in these lists or during the role call.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said the next day a new list was made out. Who would make the new list?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was we who had remained in those rooms who made these lists. Usually it was Ismet Causevic who did it. He was an art teacher, so he had very nice handwriting, and he made the list usually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the detainees make the list on their own initiative in the mornings after people, after people disappeared, or were you asked to do that by the guards?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They asked the detainees to do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guards who were in the compound, or some of the guards -- or, rather, employees from the administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that this was only -- was this true -- did this occur only in the mornings after people were taken out and disappeared, or was it every morning?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in the morning after people had been taken out during the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would these lists made in the morning show that, in fact, people had disappeared at night, and who those people would be?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We only knew about the room that we were in, our room, but we didn't have information about the other rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that -- was it true for your room, then, if people were taken out from your room, that it would be clear reading the list in the morning that certain people disappeared?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the warden of the KP Dom was when you were detained there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was Milorad Krnojelac. Before that, he was employed in the elementary school, Veselin Maslesa. He taught physics and mathematics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Krnojelac at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him twice in the compound, in the afternoon, in uniform. He was armed with a pistol. He didn't have any other weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of uniform was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What kind of uniform? A camouflage war uniform, when I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those two times when you saw him, what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was simply strolling around the compound. I don't know what his exact assignment was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who the prior warden was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The prior warden was Radojica Tesovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why he was not warden during the time that you were detained at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I cannot confirm that information because I do not know why he was replaced and why the other one was appointed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any detainees who had come from Velecevo tell you that they saw him there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They told me that they saw him up there. Whether he was in charge of that plant up there or not, he didn't know himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the detainees tell you what they saw him doing there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since there was a farm up there, there were cows and hens, et cetera, they saw him gathering eggs and packing them, I guess for selling them later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mitar Rasevic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know Mitar Rasevic. He was Commander of the guards in that camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that he was Commander of the guards?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once a piece of news leaked that an escape was being prepared from the prison, that is. The commander of the guards came with two guards to our room and he said as we talked, "We have some indications to the effect that a getaway is being prepared." I personally laughed, and I answered that question in the following way: "Where to? Out of these walls? There are guards all around." There were even two machine-guns from the administration building that were facing the rooms where the detainees were. They were pointed at us, and we could see them together with sandbags. The next day there was an order, or whatever, that Uzeir Hadzialic, also an inmate, a detainee, a locksmith, that he cut all the bars on the windows in -- on the ground floor, or rather, that he welded all the bars and the nets on the ground floor windows and on the first-floor windows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what you meant by that, that he welded these bars? Did he put -- did he install bars so that detainees would not be able to escape?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that on order of the KP Dom administration?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on somebody's orders, and who else could it have been but the administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were land mines also put in around this time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A day or two went by, I can't remember well, but it is true that a platoon of soldiers came and that they placed mines on all the lawns within the compound and around it. This is proven by the fact that there were explosions during the night. I don't know whether it was cats or dogs that activated the mines. Even a guard or an employee at the KP Dom, I'm not sure which one, was wounded, wounded in the leg. That's what we found out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you -- do you remember when this was, when Mitar Rasevic came and spoke to the detainees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It never -- oh, Mitar, I'm sorry. I thought you meant somebody else. Mitar, he talked before these bars on the windows were welded, and also before mines were placed round the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately what date or what month it was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the date. I think it was the month of June, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that a piece of news had leaked about an attempted escape. Could you tell us what that was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, before in peacetime, allegedly a prisoner escaped from that prison through a small opening in the toilet that was not sufficiently protected. That opening was in that transit room. And in all fairness, it could be used for an escape because it was on the ground floor, and one could jump out without getting hurt. And since there was quite a bit of construction material up there, it was assumed that planks could be put up, although it would involve casualties because, of course, they would shoot, right? But then on the other hand, not every bullet hits its target. However --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, was there discussion among the detainees in your room about how would could try to escape?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was not directly discussed. Everybody shrugged their shoulders. It's hard. There were guards all around, at every corner. And also, on the administration building where those weapons had been placed, there was always a guard who was on duty by these weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, what I'm interested in is the statement you made a few minutes earlier that a piece of news leaked. What was that piece of news? Did the detainees talk at some point about trying to escape, and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts that's why Mitar Rasevic came because he heard it or heard about it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this piece of news leaked about a day or two later, perhaps after he came. Whether there was a bug, I don't know. Maybe they were eavesdropping. Maybe some of the guards said it because he himself could not make such an assumption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The guards would have heard the detainees talking about methods of escape; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was a bug, they could have heard it; if not, they couldn't have. They couldn't have listened otherwise to our conversations in that room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, regarding Mr. Rasevic, I'd like to ask you about a statement that you made in 1995 to the Security Services Centre in which you said, "The duties of prison commander were performed by Mitar Rasevic." Can you explain what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The warden was the person to whom all the employees in that camp were subordinated, and Mitar Rasevic was commander of the guards. He assigned duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you about medical care for the detainees. What kind of medical care were the detainees able to obtain?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two doctors in that prison. One was a general practitioner, a detainee, and another one was a surgeon, but they couldn't perform any medical checkups on detainees. There used to come Cedo Dragovic from the hospital. He was a gynaecologist by specialisation, and detainees would come to him for medical checkups if they felt they needed one, if they felt they needed medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to get the medical care that you needed?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One time I asked to be seen by a doctor, and since I knew Dr. Cedo I went there. I had had a fever for several days. I asked him to give me some medicine. He just shrugged his shoulders and looked at a guard who was standing nearby, and he gave me a painkiller called Andol to lower my temperature. And he advised me to drink as much fluid as possible. However, I couldn't get much tea to drink because all the tea we got was at breakfast and dinner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were detainees who did not have acquaintances or connections from the hospital, were they able to get medicines and things like that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went for checkups. They were seen by a doctor, but I don't know what they received in terms of medication. I didn't see it, so I cannot say. I swore before this court to speak the truth, and I'm speaking the truth only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Yesterday you talked about some work groups. Were there also some detainees taken to work at a fishpond in Jelec?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That fishpond was kept by the prison in peacetime, and then when the occupation and military operation started, they were afraid that this fishpond would run to seed. So a work group once went there to catch the larger fish and put them up for sale at the market.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in end April or early May, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if work groups went to the fishpond later in the summer, or was that the only time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was once or twice that they went there. All I know from those who had been there is that they released the fish into the rivers, Govza and another river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of the summer, did any work groups go further to catch fish or work at any fishponds as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that they were catching or fishing. I know about groups who went to unload flour from mills in Ustikolina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we don't need --

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also until before the end -- before mid-May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We don't need to hear about that any further; we have other witnesses who have given us that evidence already. Let me ask you about blood donations. Were detainees ever asked to make blood donations, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned when I was speaking about the wounding of the warden's sons in Bota during the explosion, a medical technician appeared at the KP Dom on that day. He served under Bota, I believe, and he asked whether anyone wanted to volunteer for donating blood. People gave a large amount of blood. I believe there were 70 donors or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that they asked for volunteers. Were the detainees promised anything in return for giving blood?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they had been promised anything, but I do know that they eventually received a pack of cigarettes and a small tin of canned meat, perhaps 100 or 150 grams a can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times were people requested to give blood?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That lasted for a number of days. A team from the medical centre was coming for several days running to take the blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give blood?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did a television crew ever come to the KP Dom, and if so, were they allowed to speak with the detainees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, sometime in July, in the beginning of July, a team of journalists came, and among them were some foreigners, and outside Rooms 11 and 13 they stood without going in. They wanted to talk to us detainees. There was Dr. Torlak in our room who spoke some English, and there was a Gordan Mujicic, we called his Gordo, who spoke French well. Standing at the window, we shouted, Gordo specifically shouted and waved his hands, motioning the journalists to come closer, and the woman who was an anchor in television - I know her because she was a teacher -- a pupil of my mother's, my mother was a teacher. Her last name was Gigovic. She was Vesna Gigovic. She waved her hand and the guards commander, Rasevic, came then and turned the team away. They didn't allow them to come closer to our rooms and talk to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this team, the TV crew, was it then a Yugoslav crew, or was it a foreign crew, English speaking?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what language they spoke. We assumed that perhaps it might be a foreign television crew, and therefore the people among us who could speak foreign languages came forward. But I knew this one journalist who worked in Novi Sad, and there was a crew from the Novi Sad television station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, during the more than four months that you were detained at KP Dom, can you tell us how your health was affected?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I weighed around 100 kilos, or perhaps between 89 and 100 kilos, and after I was released, I lost -- I'd lost 14 kilos. And I suffer from obstructive nephritis and I have to use medication all the time, and I'm suffering from a strong spasm in that area. That's as far as my health is concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, can you tell us how this detention affected you psychologically?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to explain it to you. When I was once again among normal people, they seemed to look at me all the time. They seemed to think I was too thin. It seems I'd lost a lot of weight, perhaps, because I was resettled in a community where there had been no military operations. Novi Pazar, Niksic, and that's where I spent the rest of my time before returning to Sarajevo in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, those are the questions of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Vasic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am Milorad Vasic, one of the Defence counsel of the accused Krnojelac. Sir, during your examination-in-chief, you told us the address at which you resided in Foca before the start of military operations. Can you tell us which part of town it was where you lived? Will you just please wait for the interpreters to interpret our question and then make a pause before answering so that our participants can hear the interpretation of my question and your answer properly.

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that at the beginning of the conflict, some houses owned by ethnic Serbs burnt down, including the house of Milorad Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I was still working, and I heard the news that some buildings had burnt down not far away from the hospital, including some houses near the health centre; but as far as Milorad Krnojelac's house is concerned, I hadn't heard anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You said that after being away from work you came back to the institution where you were employed. Did you see any road blocks in Donje Polje at the time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was down there, I didn't see anything except for a vehicle down there at the bridge. Whether it was a road block or just a vehicle, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any persons around the vehicle at the time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my side of this passage from the medical centre -- from my house to the medical centre, no, there weren't any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your examination-in-chief, you said that Serbian forces walked in to the institution where you worked after a couple of days because no resistance was offered?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wasn't any resistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please wait a little for two reasons: For other people to hear the interpretation, and second, your voice is protected and while my microphone is turned on, there can be no voice distortion. If you look at the monitor in front of you, you will be able to follow --

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is nothing whatsoever on my monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we're trying to enable this voice distortion as far as we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Protect the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll have it turned on for the transcript. Now, sir, you'll see in front of you a transcript, and the Court reporter here is typing the translation so that when the typing finishes you know the translation has finished. So just wait until you see the typing finish before you answer any question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question. So you said during your examination-in-chief that Serb forces, after a couple of days, walked into the hospital because there was no resistance there. My question is, why didn't they enter that institution earlier if, as you say, there was no resistance?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the reason. Perhaps there was some protection, some defence lines in the outer circle like the Mijakovici village. Maybe they couldn't get in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it mean that in the wider area of Donje Polje there was resistance on the part of ethnic Bosniaks and that is the reason why they hadn't entered earlier?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: People who had personal weapons may have tried to defend themselves because they were in danger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that at the beginning of the conflict, in April of 1992, there were Muslim military units at the KP Dom for a while?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why are you so sure that they -- that there hadn't been any? Did you have occasion to see the KP Dom and who occupied it before Serb forces took over this part of Donje Polje?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked whether Muslim forces had been at the hospital, and I maintain that there hadn't been any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about the hospital. I said, is it true that in April 1992, at the beginning of the conflict, there were Muslim forces at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statements I stated that I went to hospital, to the hospital [redacted] on the 10th of April, and that from that time on I had no information as to where anyone was, and I couldn't claim anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how far is this hospital from the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 800 metres away, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were at the hospital, did you have opportunity to hear about fighting taking place nearby?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shooting could be heard, of course, and another proof of fighting is the arrival of wounded people that I mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It is true you stated in your examination-in-chief that at that time, it was mainly civilians who were brought to the hospital. Who except civilians was brought?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one else after the hospital was taken over by occupying forces, [redacted] the time. When the forces entered the hospital, I can't say whether it was three or four days later, two uniformed persons of Serbian ethnicity were brought. In fact, one of them was an ethnic Hungarian, and he was an alcoholic, delirious at the time. And when I talked to him he told me he was a professional soldier, that he had been on the battlefield for eight years, that he had been on all front lines in all the wars. Another case that I remember was a younger man, a disabled man. His right arm was missing. He was also armed. I was so afraid that I didn't dare ask him even his name. I was afraid that something bad might happen to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me, in which language did you speak to that ethnic Hungarian?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our language, the Bosnian language, the Serbo-Croat. He could speak it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. During your examination-in-chief you mentioned that soldiers had brought Mr. Salimovic and Mr. Cankusic to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the date when that happened?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly whether it was the 17th or the 18th of April, one of those two days for sure. And maybe ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that Dr. Supic wanted to keep these persons in hospital. Can you tell me what is Dr. Supic from an ethnic point of view?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is a Serb, and he's a professional, and he carried out his duties in a professional manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us what regrettably happened to these persons, and you said that you saw these persons while Dr. Zijo Ajanovic was identifying the persons who were killed. Who were the persons that were then identified by Dr. Ajanovic, do you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These persons, in addition to Cankusic and Selimovic, the ones I mentioned are Isanovic, Delic, Sandal, and the one who was shot at in front of the hospital who fell into the cemetery at Patkovina, Sejdin, a younger man, and also Bostandzic. Those are the corpses that I personally saw at the morgue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, in the second statement you gave to the investigators of the OTP in 1999, did you say that persons between the age of 16 and 75 were arrested and taken to the KP Dom, and persons who did not belong to a single political party or those who were very old or who were not considered dangerous were allowed to stay at home? Is that what you stated? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, out of the detainees who arrived in the camp, there were persons belonging to various groups, young, elderly, there were some who were even older than I was, considerably older. As for town, I did not realise whether there were any men left, whether there was anyone except for women and children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But on page 2 of your statement from 1999 it says that you stated the following. Would it help you if I read it out to you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there is such a piece of paper, I would like to see it, and I would like to see what I said and where.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is document ID 298, and also 298A. The B/C/S version, paragraph 3, second sentence: "Persons between the age of 16 and 75 were arrested and taken to the KP Dom, while people who did not belong to a single political party or those who were very old and not considered dangerous were allowed to stay at home."

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that a group of older people were released from prison at the beginning of May. I don't know whether I mentioned all of that. Among these persons are some survivors as well, but those persons had to report every day to the SUP. That's the statement I made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Was communication between detainees at the KP Dom prohibited, and was it restricted to persons who were staying in the same room only?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Communication among detainees in the KP Dom was prohibited. We never got out of the rooms except for breakfast, lunch, and dinner. We only communicated amongst ourselves in our rooms, except for the persons who went out to work. They managed to have contacts. Later, the persons from all rooms were taken to one room, that is to say, persons who worked. They were all supposed to be together so that they would not have any contacts with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your assumption, that they were separated into one room so that they would not have contact with you, or do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that because persons from my room who worked were taken to this separate room, and they could be seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Weren't people who worked singled out and put into one room so that they would be concentrated all in one place, not so that they would be isolated from contact with other detainees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both, because those who went out, they could get information from citizens, other citizens outside, and they could convey this information to us. That's what they were afraid of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Tell me, please, until the 15th of May, 1992, were visits allowed by family members to detainees at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were detainees allowed to receive clothes and food?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clothes, yes, but under strict control rules -- food with strict control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean provided that there was strict control over what was brought?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, strict control. Not in the rooms. Detainees were taken out to a special separate room for that by the entrance into the administration building, and not in larger groups or anything. The maximum was two detainees, and the family members who came to visit them, and this was once in 15 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these rooms for visits?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the person -- as for the purpose, well, this was just a room on the right-hand side when you enter the hallway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, while you were at the KP Dom, did you take showers?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In four months while I was there, we had only three organised baths, only three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In response to my learned friend's questions, you spoke about medical care. Were you visited by a doctor at the KP Dom once a week?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once, yes, but perhaps even more because I did not report to a doctor during that interval. I cannot say with 100 per cent certainty whether there were other people from the room reporting to the doctor, but I can confirm that the doctor came in once a week.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you state to the investigator of the OTP that at first prisoners got eggs and pate for breakfast, and that then this stopped?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first we would sometimes get one egg, one slice of bread, and tea, which was not really sweet; and then the next day we would get a can of pate which would be shared between two prisoners. At any rate, a loaf of bread weighing 650 grams was sliced into ten slices. Now, you divide that by ten, so you see how much you get, 6 and a half grams.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You talked about blood donations today in response to my colleague's questions, and you said that that had to do with the wounding of a person named Bota and the sons of Milorad Krnojelac. Why did you not mention this until now in your statements?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how the questions were put, in which order, but I stated that during every interview I had, whoever I talked to. How these Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts corrections were made, I don't know in relation to this last question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statements, either in the one you made to the state security station in Konjic or in the two statements that you gave to the State Commission for Collecting Facts about War Crimes, or in the two statements that you gave to the investigators of the OTP, is there any mention that blood donations were given because of this? Did you talk about it at all during your interviews then?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim now and in response to these questions that were put, on all four occasions, if I was asked -- I mean, it's been nine years and memory fades, but I stand by this. Before blood had never been required from the detainees until that moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were detainees donating blood at the KP Dom? Can you give us the date?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in mid-June. I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this happen during the first half of June?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it is the first half of June or mid-June. I can't say. It's been a lot of time since then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the persons you mentioned injured in the same accident?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you refer -- are you referring to Bota and also to his sons?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information we received, it was the same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that a person called Bota together with a military policeman was injured on the 17th or 18th of June when he fell into an ambush and was wounded by a bullet?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I never mentioned that anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the sons of Milorad Krnojelac were injured during another accident when they, together with nine other persons, were in a truck that hit a mine?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information we got was that they entered a minefield somewhere around Tjentiste.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that this event took place five or six days after the event concerning the person nicknamed Bota took place?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. In response to my learned friend's questions, you said that you were interrogated in the KP Dom, first by an interrogator who was called Koprivica, and then by an interrogator called Vladicic. Do you know that a person called Zoran Vukovic, who was chief of the military police, also carried out investigations at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally do not know Zoran Vukovic. I personally was interrogated by Vladicic, and Koprivica had actually started and then that was interrupted, and then Vladicic finished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In response to my learned friend's questions yesterday and today, you spoke about the lists that you made. In addition to the list of persons who were taken out in groups from the KP Dom Foca between the 26th of June until the 15th of July, 1992, and the list of persons who were taken out that is marked ID 301 and that relates to the month of August, did you also make a list of employees in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could remember. I did make a list of those who I remembered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you compile this list of employees from the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just after I got out of prison while I still remembered these persons, because time makes you forget. I could not list all of them now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means in 1992?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In part of this list that is called "inspectors, investigators," in addition to Zoran Vladicic and Koprivica, nicknamed Kopi, you also mentioned Zoran Vukovic for the military police.

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned that because he is chief of the military police. That's what I heard. But he did not interrogate me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He Did not interrogate you, but he was an investigator at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that I did not know him, nor do I know who that man is. I don't know him until the present day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you then explain how come his name appeared on the list of investigators that you compiled in 1992 if you don't know him and if you don't know who he is?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other persons told me that he was chief of the military police in town and that he brought into custody many, many persons who were in prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you talk to these persons who gave you information about Zoran Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we got out of prison. The group of those who survived, together with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you talk to them, in which place?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Novi Pazar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who are the persons with whom you talked about details related to the KP Dom in Novi Pazar in 1992?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The persons who got out with me. The persons who got out with me to Novi Pazar. There were 35 of us who had left Foca and reached Rozaje. About ten remained in Rozaje as they found their families there. The rest, 22, 23, 25, I'm not sure, since there wasn't enough room there for us to be accommodated, we were transferred to Novi Pazar to a centre there called Rajcinovic Banja. We found quite a few refugees from Foca there, and all these refugees started asking about their own family members as to where they are and whether they had survived. So there was a lot of talking going on. As for the people who were with me, there was Asim Cankusic, Hadzimuratovic. He was a forwarder from Gornje Polje. And another Hadzimuratovic from Jelec. Then Juso Cemo, Almas Kruho, Rahman Salkija, and another Rahman, Fajko Tafro -- Faik Tafro, Safet Kumro, and I cannot remember the rest right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. So after these conversations and after this exchange of information, you compiled a list of employees at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of conversations and joint memory, did you compile the other list that my learned friend asked you about here in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean these lists of persons who were taken out of the camp?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the list of employees at the KP Dom, did you say that Savo Todovic is an interrogator who is responsible for a lot of mistreatment of Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that about Savo Todovic. I just knew that he was allegedly the assistant warden, and that he knew what happened, just like the warden did with these persons who were no longer there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I remind you, sir, to watch that screen before you answer the question. You have been doing very well, but that answer came in a long way before the interpreters had finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This list of employees at the KP Dom that you compiled, as you said, on the basis of conversations you had with other persons who left the KP Dom, is that the opinion based on the conversations that you had with other persons that you mentioned under number 3, Savo Todovic, an investigator responsible for a lot of mistreatment and killings of Bosniak civilians?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. During your interrogation at the KP Dom, did the investigator ask you about whether you knew about Bosniak Muslim persons who had stolen medicines from the hospital in Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he asked me about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, did Inspector Vladicic, after he concluded his questioning, did he say that you would be taken to trial? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me explain about the medicines. He asked me where the medicine [redacted] had gone, and also [redacted]. My answer was that I did not use medicine, or rather, that I did not distribute it. I just asked for medicine for time to time [redacted] [redacted]. And then I said that he had to inquire in the pharmacy as to who had been given these large quantities of medicine. During the interrogation, as it ended, when he offered me this statement so that I could sign it, I tried to read it, but he warned me that I should sign it without reading it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He warned me that this would be taken to court, and he also asked me whether I wanted him to write down that I had killed ten persons as well. And I said that he can write whatever he wants to, that I was in his hands, and that I was powerless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already explained that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm afraid it's 11.00 so perhaps it would be a good time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. There will be a reference in his third last answer that will have to be redacted, but I'll make sure that's done during the adjournment so that it will not be broadcast. We'll resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in response to my learned friend's question about persons whom you say were taken out on the 26th and 27th and taken perhaps to Bileca to a court martial, were you saying that it was a military court martial?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information to the effect that it was a court martial. They only said that the court has been established in Foca. That was the information broadcast by the media. That was my response to the question, whether it existed or not, whether somebody had ordered for somebody to deliver those people to that court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement given to the State Commission for Collecting Facts on War Crimes, on the 23rd September 1992, did you say that the persons taken away from the KP Dom to Bileca to court martial, and in another version, that they were killed?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that statement I said that those persons, as far as I was able to find out, were taken for exchanges because there was a front line then at -- near Dubrovnik, and my information was that those people were being exchanged and that those people had never been heard from again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you state that you had heard that those people had perhaps been taken to Bileca to a military court martial?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have the same problem as a couple of days ago. We don't hear everyone on channel 7, so I may have lost the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Vasic. We have a problem here. The interpreters did not hear the answer to that question. Perhaps you should ask him to -- ask him the question again, unless you can recall what his answer was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll ask my question again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say to the State Commission for Collecting Facts on War Crimes that persons who were taken away from the KP Dom on the 26th February were taken perhaps to the court martial, and in another version, that they may have been killed?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said not only about the persons who were taken out on the 25th of June, but persons who were on the longer list, who were taken out in smaller groups, that I had information that they may have been taken for an exchange to the Dubrovnik front, and because Mate Vancic was among those people, and Kruno, who dabbled in journalism, they were not of the same ethnicity. And I doubted it could have been true. I -- perhaps it was true, perhaps not. Maybe the accused can tell the Honourable Court where these people are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know a person by the name of Dzevad Smajkan?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Sacir Smajkan, but not Dzevad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Sacir Smajkan had been detained in the Ministry of the Interior of Trebinje, the SUP of Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no such information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Did you state to investigators of the office of the Prosecutor that those who were going to work considered themselves lucky because they received food in addition to what they were getting at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We considered that they were in an advantageous position because they had opportunity to contact more people, maybe even some people from the town. And if nothing else, fruit was available then in July and August, and they could eat more. We learnt from them that they got an extra meal called "snack" while we did not have that and we were starving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. We discussed already today the lists that you have drawn up, lists of people who had been taken out. Can you tell me about these people who were taken in groups from the KP Dom from the 26th of June to the 15th of July, ID 299? When did you draw it up, in 1992 when you were released, or after your return in 1995?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drew up that list immediately after I got out of prison while I still had a fresh memory because I knew those people, and as everyone knows, time means forgetting. I could have probably listed more of them if I had known what had happened to those people. As far as I know, those people in larger groups were saying they were going to be exchanged. I hadn't known that then. As for smaller groups who were taken out during the night, I came to the conclusion that they were killed. And from what I know, shots were heard, screaming, and moaning, and sounds of beating, and for all I know, they have never been heard from again. They never reappeared again. And I am asking this Honourable Court to have the accused tell us where these people are so that they can give -- so that they can be given a proper burial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, I understand your concern about this matter, but that is not something that really can we do in the course of your evidence, so will you please just get on with your evidence and leave that point to one side.

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you possess the original of this list, because you said these were copies?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The list I had yesterday is the original. Maybe I haven't included everyone in that list because I didn't see everything. Maybe other people can give some more information. The number may be larger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this list, the photocopy of which you handed over to investigators of the OTP, the lists of people taken out from June to July, corresponds to the list made in 1995?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does, except for the part which concerns Uzeir Cankusic, Adnan Isanovic, and another person. Those people were shot outside the hospital in the beginning. I think they are in the list as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, it says so in the list, but I'm interested in something else. On which typewriter did you type this list and where?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Novi Pazar in one of the socially-owned premises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a typewriter, or was it a computer?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: An ordinary typewriter. I had a handwritten list which I destroyed after I typed it out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were drawing up and typing that list, were you alone, or were you in the company of other former detainees who left the KP Dom together with you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I had a list written in pencil, I was alone when I read that list and gave it to a typist who typed it. And I can say that Dzemo, Vahida, should also be on the list and is not included.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Concerning the list of people taken out in August about which you told us that it was drawn up in 1997 [Realtime transcript read in error "1992"], is it your handwriting, or is it somebody else's?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry to interrupt, but there's a discrepancy in what the question was and what's on the transcript, but I also think there was a factual error in that. Mr. Vasic said 1997, the transcript shows 1992, but in fact I think it was 1992. So perhaps we could have that question asked to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps we should ask you what your qualifications are in - I hope I get the letters right - B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: But the translation, Your Honour, said 1997. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The translation, I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And the transcript says 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But you say it should be 1992 anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Factually I think it should be 1992 because that's what I understood from the Witness's testimony. So I don't know whether the translation, which I heard, was somebody who misspoke 1997, or whether in fact Mr. Vasic did say 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that. Mr. Vasic, which did you intend?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in response to my learned friend's question during examination-in-chief, the Witness said that he made this list after his return to Bosnia, according to the information. He got together with former detainees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you make this list of people who were taken out from the KP Dom between the 25th of June and the 27th of August, and on the 31st of August?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What I asked you was, did you say in 1997, and if you did say it, did you intend to say it? And are you disputing Ms. Kuo's suggestion that the witness had spoken about 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said 1997, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You see, earlier you said in answer to -- you asked a question, page 34, lines 5 and 6, "When did you draw it up, in 1992 when you were released, or after your return in 1995?" And the answer was, "I draw up that list immediately after I got out of prison whilst I still had a fresh memory." That suggests he was accepting 1992 as his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but we're talking about a list ID 299, the list of people who were taken out between the 26th of June and 15th of July. I'm not asking him about list ID 301, a list of people who were taken out in August 1992, when that list was made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: A different list. Well, Ms. Kuo, does that satisfied your query?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The -- I don't believe the witness ever said 1997, so that question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The first thing to do is to ascertain from the witness when the second list was drawn up. And then we should all be happy, I hope. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the list of people who were taken out in August 1992, when did you make it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made that list several times. Among other things, it was mentioned in the statement to the Secretariat of the Interior of Konjic upon my return the first time, the second time at the investigator's in Sarajevo on two occasions, the third time when I was talking to the State Commission for Tracing Missing Persons. That was the fourth time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm talking about the list presented to you by my learned friend which is number ID 301 which you read out at her request. When did you make this list?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made all those lists when I was giving my statements to investigators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which year was that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1997, one; and the other one at the Secretariat of the Interior in Konjic was in 1995. I don't remember about the third. One list I made at the state commission in 1996. I wouldn't be able to tell you about the sequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the help of the usher, I would like to show this witness list number ID 301, because I'm asking only about one of the lists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, is it true that it's your handwriting on this list?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is my handwriting exactly. This first group in the upper part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have explained that already.

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It relates to the departure of two groups on the 25th and the 27th. A group of about 36 to 40 people in total taken out in groups of 20 on the 25th, and the 27th. And this third part relates to the group which got out together with me and was returned once to the prison, and then groups of ten were singled out, and out of those people, none has ever been heard from again. In total, that would be about 60 persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, sir, that this third list relates to intellectuals.

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And there are more of them, about 20.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said this was your handwriting. In response to my learned friend's question, however, you said you dictated this list. How come you dictated something which is written in your own hand?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I dictated at first, and then I made my own list in my own hand knowing that I would be coming here to testify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you please look at page 2 of this document, ID 301. That's the group which you say are intellectuals who were taken out. Can you tell me the profession of Mr. Avdo Kameric?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Avdo Kameric is not in the group of intellectuals, but he's a highly skilled worker, craftsman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the occupations of Pace, the father and son, that's second line from the top in document ID 301?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. This list here is not of intellectuals. This is a list of the people who were separated from us after we got back from Niksic to the KP Dom, except for Avdo Kameric and Fadil Divjan. This list here relates partly to intellectuals and partly to highly-skilled workers. I remember some more intellectuals which I could add to the list if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you speaking about this list when you said to my learned friend that the people listed were intellectuals?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are some intellectuals, and I even failed to list all of them. I could add some more. I said so in response to the Prosecutor's question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From this list, the name of Balic Dzemo, what was his occupation? You say here he was a trader.

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a trader, but I don't know that he is on the list of intellectuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at page 2 of document ID 301, the fourth line is Balic, Dzemo, a trader.

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is a trader, but I don't know that all the intellectuals are listed here. Some names are missing. I don't know how this came about. I can now individually enumerate these individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is a person with the last name of Veiz also on the list, and a person under number six who is an employee of Maglic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked on repairs. He repaired the building of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain, sir, why, when you were making this list, you failed to mention all the people which you now say you could enumerate? Was your memory in 1997 better than now in 2001 as far as events in the KP Dom are concerned? And you said you were doing this while your memory was still fresh so that you wouldn't forget.

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, I wasn't thinking about intellectuals. I never made this statement before 1996. I gave this statement subsequently while I was thinking why so many intellectuals were missing? Was it on purpose that these people were killed, this very able workforce of young, educated people who went missing during the war years?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, out of the eight people who are on the list, the people whom you call intellectuals, four are intellectuals and four are skilled workers. Do you still call this a list of intellectuals?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't know really how this came about, this discrepancy between statements. I can now enumerate the intellectuals before Honourable Court and I cold even say where each of them is employed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Today you mentioned that from the administrative building, machine-guns were pointed at the prisoners' quarters. Why did you fail to mention this in all the statements you made before, to the security station, to the Secretariat of the Interior, and the two statements you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was giving those statements, in all of them, I couldn't mention even a third of what had happened. A person isn't able to concentrate. He is under emotional pressure, in an emotional state, and it takes you over. And from the administrative building pointed towards the garages in the prisoners' building, I saw Brdjo on two occasions, a man I knew, and Kruno. They worked shifts. In the other part I just saw machine-guns; I couldn't see any faces. And a lot of time has gone by, and a person tends to remember some things and fails to remember other things. And from all the people who come here before the Tribunal, Honourable Court, you will see that all of them saw things differently. The room where I was, was on the ground floor, and I couldn't see a lot of things that could be seen by other people who were on upper floors, people who were in rooms facing the town, people who had a view, and some of them could even see what was going on outside within the prison itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in response to my learned friend's question, you also said for the first time today that on two occasions when you saw Milorad Krnojelac in the KP Dom, you saw him carrying a pistol. You didn't mention that in any of the statements you gave before. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody asked me whether he was armed or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I couldn't agree with you, sir, that nobody had asked you whether he had been armed or not. In your statement of 31 May 1999, given to the investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor, you stated, "I don't know whether or not he had personal weapons."

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, I thought that what they meant was bigger weapons. I didn't think they meant personal weapons, smaller firearms, because a license is required for hunting rifles and things like that. I didn't think that licenses were needed for automatic weapons and personal weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, that's exactly what I was saying, that you were talking about personal weapons, not about automatic rifles, big rifles, things like that. You said that you were not aware of whether Milorad Krnojelac had personal weapons.

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can say that he had nothing, but I was 30 or 50 metres away from him. I saw a holster. Of course it was a pistol that he had. What else could he have had?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to read that part to you. That is document ID 298. The B/C/S version is 298A. In B/C/S it is page 4, paragraph 1; in the English version it is also page 4. In the paragraph where you speak about Milorad Krnojelac: "Milorad Krnojelac was the warden, the camp warden, and before he took over this duty at the KP Dom, he was a mathematics teacher." And now the part that is of interest to us: "A few times when I saw him, he wore a camouflage uniform. I don't know whether he wore -- he carried any personal weapons." Is this what you stated to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I mentioned personal weapons. I just know about the pistol, that he carried a pistol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were giving this statement on the 31st of May, 1999, did the investigator from the OTP put a question to you that -- whether you saw Milorad Krnojelac at the KP Dom carrying any weapons?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which weapons this related to. I don't know. I answered that I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Today when my learned friend asked you whether you saw Mr. Krnojelac at the KP Dom, why did you say that he had a pistol, and she never even asked you about it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw what I saw, and I maintain that he had a pistol. I cannot confirm what kind of an assignment he had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In response to my learned friend's question, you said today, sir, that a person had been wounded in the leg from the mines that were placed around the KP Dom. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172 [Resumed]
